Question: What were the reasons for Germany's defeat in World War II despite having superior weapons such as Panzer tanks and ME-109 fighters?
Answer: Being able to build one superior weapon is totally irrelevant. What matters is the ability to build superior weapons at an industrial scale and bring them to where they are needed, fully equipped and crewed. Nazi Germany could not do that. Nazi Germany was pulled by horses. Nazi Germany totally sucked at logistics. The Soviets could build sort of crappy weapons at industrial scales, even insane scales, and bring them to where they were needed, halfway equipped and with a skeleton crew. That’s quite enough to win you a war against someone who has a dozen ME-109 fighters stuck at the factory for lack of rubber for the wheels, and another dozen sitting in a airfield for lack of fuel. Soviet tanks often only lasted about 100km before they fell apart, but that didn’t matter; there was already another one rolling off the production line. A Panzer tank was a fine weapon, but it was still toast when it faced ten Soviet tanks, even if the Soviet tanks had welding so poor there were actual gaps in the plating. Ten crossbows will defeat a rifle, especially when the rifle has a tendency to jam.

Question: I bought a top sirloin to cook at home, cooked one half and placed the other half in the fridge for tomorrow. Patches of my steak turned greyish overnight. Did it partially rot overnight?
Answer: Absolutely not. It rusted. Yep, that’s what happens. The meat is red because it contains haemoglobin, the same substance that makes blood red. (It will also contain small amounts of actual blood, yes.) It is red because it contains free iron. When it’s exposed to air, it absorbs oxygen – in essence, it rusts, and goes a dull brown or vaguely greyish. Meat that has started to rot will of course have that colour. But the colour change happens overnight, while rotting takes far longer. What you do is to smell it. The human nose is pretty good at smelling out when food has gone bad, as long as it’s food that’s roughly the same stuff as we’d be able to lay our hands on “in the wild”, like fresh meat and berries. Rotting meat stinks to high heaven. You’d probably need to clean the fridge to get rid of the smell. If your steak has only been in the fridge overnight, I wouldn’t even bother smelling it unless it was already beyond its sell-by date. It’s fine to eat.

Question: Did Ukraine’s plan at forcing Russia to redeploy troops from eastern Ukraine to Kursk fail?

It’s basically re-deploy or get hammered. Because it’s not only about the political fallout of Russia having been invaded, and Russia failing completely to do anything about it. It’s also about cutting off supply routes to Donbass. If you look at a map and use a ruler, you find that Russian supply routes are now comfortably within range of Ukrainian HiMars units in Kursk. Russia is going all in in Donbass, because they know they have to achieve their immediate tactical objectives with what they’ve got there. There is no more “slow grind”, it’s do or die (or, increasingly, both). And if they manage that, they then have to turn north and oust Ukraine from Kursk, still only with what they’ve already got there. So it only “failed” in the sense that Russia didn’t do what they rationally had to do. Since Russia didn’t do that, Russia is essentially betting the entire outcome of the war on delivering those two objectives. At this point, I’m not sure whether they even believe in it themselves; so far in the war, they haven’t had a grip on Ukrainian capabilities, and they seem to have had a very poor grip even on their own capabilities, so they might have drawn the conclusion that they can pull it off, but in that case, based on poor quality information. (They might still be right, though.) They might also just have received orders to achieve this, and stopping to consider whether an order is even realistic isn’t in the Russian military mindset. So… wait and see. One possible outcome is that Russia just barely manages to reach Pokrovsk, but Ukraine manages to advance slowly in Kursk; being cut off from any significant supplies and reinforcements, Russian troops in western Donbass are then forced to surrender or flee, collapsing the entire effort.

Question: How deadly would something like the common cold be to an alien whose immune system isn’t adapted to it?
Answer: If the alien has an immune system at all (and it’s hard to imagine how it could be alive without having one; it needs a way to separate things that belong in the body from things that don’t), it will do basically the same thing that ours does: destroy anything that doesn’t have very specific chemical markers that say it is a part of our body. The virus that causes the common cold will not have those markers saying “I’m an alien body part”. It has evolved over thousands and millions of years to have the markers that say “I’m a human body part”. It will be eliminated in no time flat. It will be very much like the tobacco mosaic virus trying to infect a human. Nothing will happen; it will not even recognise human cells as living. Bacteria might be different, especially if they by chance excrete something that’s a deadly toxin to the aliens. Bacteria are alive in a way viruses aren’t, having a metabolism of their own, and can grow in rather hostile conditions as long as their favourite “foods” are present. I’m not taking bets on it, though; most bacteria that thrive on humans are also very specifically adapted to do so, and the vast majority of bacteria on Earth are simply killed by our immune systems without further ado. Fundamentally, this is how it works: Immune systems are designed to destroy any intruder. >99.9% of the time, it’s viruses that have to adapt to us to bypass our immune systems, not the other way around.

Question: To do with nuclear weapons in space. I was under the impression that nuclear weapons lost their potency after a few months, and required ‘charging’ from - possibly- a reactor - to keep them viable - is there any truth in this?
Answer: No, that’s mixing up two totally different things. Most modern nuclear weapons use plutonium as fissile material. That decays at a rate that requires the charge to be replaced every 30 years or so. (The old charge can then be processed and have most of it recycled into a new charge.) Hydrogen bombs need to have the fusion charge replaced more often, every few years. Nuclear missiles, though, are propelled by ordinary rocket fuel, with a shelf life of some six months. You would normally not even want it in the missile; it has a tendency to be corrosive, so you fuel the missile when you think you might want to use it soon. For nuclear weapons in space, you’d probably work out something else – preferably a solid fuel, since it gets a bit cold. But yes, it’s a headache anyway. You need to lift large amounts of fuel with extreme shelf life up into orbit, and then going down, it’s necessarily going to be a bit inaccurate as far as aiming goes. It’s actually very hard to see that there would be any major benefits to having nuclear weapons in space. You wouldn’t be able to hide them, they’re not all that easy to aim, the logistics of replacing charges and fuel are enormously complex, it is – counter-intuitively – likely to take them longer to arrive at their destination, they’re going to have to stay up instead of just being lobbed from Earth’s surface and fall down of their own accord… far better to have them in missile silos, easy to get at, not in plain sight, can be protected against other nukes, and so on.

Question: Why is depleted uranium rather than enriched uranium used in armor piercing bullets and shells? I know depleted is cheaper but would not enriched be more deadly?
Answer: No. Depleted uranium has a half-life of some 4.5 billion years. This is no more radioactive than that you can make your underwear out of it and suffer no ill effects. OK that isn’t literally true, U-238 decays by emitting alpha particles: it’s stopped by the skin, but you don’t want to inhale the stuff because it can cause lung cancer, so you shouldn’t stuff it up your nose, and having it next to your body it might give off tiny particles that might be inhaled. But U-238 is the second least radioactive element we’ve found in any significant amounts. If you’re being shot at with the stuff, the radioactivity is less of a concern than basically anything else – sunstroke, the soldier next to you having Covid, having a traffic accident on the way back to base, sharks in your bathtub, anything. Weapons-grade highly enriched uranium is about 90% U-235, and has a half-life of 700 million years. It’s the fourth least radioactive element we’ve found in any significant amounts. The thing is that even if you quadruple the radioactivity of the bullet, it goes from totally insignificant to slightly less totally insignificant – still totally insignificant, just measurably less insignificant. Don’t sniff it and you’ll be fine.

Question: A question for westerners. When is Russia's economy going to collapse according to Western knowledge? 2025 is approaching and there's no sign of collapse in Russia.

There are plenty of signs that Russia’s economy is under severe strain, even in Kremlin’s propaganda reports. Inflation is said to be at 9%, but interest rates are 18%, which indicates that the inflation figures are “adjusted” and are probably some 12–15%. The spread in buy/sell rates for USD is insane, like a 10x difference. Production of consumer goods has collapsed and Russia is forced to sell oil and LNG to China and India at steep discount. Food prices have skyrocketed and pensions have stayed the same. There is no money for repair of infrastructure. The only thing keeping the Russian economy afloat now is unfunded military spending, and that’s basically throwing good money after bad: public investment in infrastructure can be a good thing even if it brings budget deficits in its wake, since the roads and irrigation and power cables and whatever is a benefit for the economy. In contrast, money spent on things that you just blow up, like missiles, doesn’t bring any benefits, you’re just throwing your money into a hole. Economic collapse rarely happens overnight. Even the infamous collapse of 1929 took over two weeks, and it took over a year for it to lead to the Great Depression. The Russian collapse has started, and by the time it makes headlines it’ll be impossible to stop.

Question: Can anesthesia refuse to put you to sleep for surgery because your doctor says you’re too old for surgery? I'm 62 years old and my cardiologist says my heart is strong.
Answer: Yes, the anaesthesiologist has the responsibility for your body being able to take the strain of anaesthesia and surgery. There must be some other issue; the heart isn’t all that needs to be in decent shape for surgery. Today, for instance, many refuse to perform surgery on smokers who haven’t been off the cigarettes for at least a couple of weeks, due to the dramatically increased risks of complications in active smokers. Liver and kidneys also need to be in as good shape as possible – they handle all medications that enter the body. Whatever the issue is, it must have to do with the “otherwise healthy” part.

Question: Who is winning the war in Ukraine, NATO-funded Ukraine or Russia?
Answer: Russia has already lost the war; all that remains to see is exactly how badly. Even if Russia manages to occupy all of Ukraine, they will have lost. It will just take longer for it to become obvious. Russia’s goal was to turn Ukraine into a copy of Belarus: independent in name only, ruled by a Russian puppet, with money flowing out from Ukraine and into the pockets of oligarchs. The actual oppression would be left to an Ukrainian FSB branch. This will obviously never happen. Russia can, at best, achieve a permanent military occupation, with at least 1 million soldiers doing nothing but oppressing Ukrainians, costing them as much money as the entire pre-2022 Russian military, in addition to the regular military budget. This is totally unsustainable and will bankrupt Russia, without even taking into account how the Russian industry is already suffering from lack of workforce. In addition, there will be a NATO-supported permanent insurgency: think Afghanistan, only Ukrainians can travel all over Russia and perform sabotage anywhere. Eventually, Russia will be forced to withdraw, just like the Soviets withdrew from Afghanistan. The only question is whether they will do so in some semblance of order, or whether the collapse will be as messy and chaotic as the dissolution of the USSR. The military side of it is actually quite secondary. Those are forces of economy and politics, decided by factors outside Russia’s control. As for Ukraine, the end result will be an independent country. Either by the current regime surviving, or by an independent regime being established when Russia collapses. In that sense, Ukraine has already won.

Question: How did Hitler and Nazi Germany arm itself to the teeth for the upcoming World War II in the midst of a worldwide depression in the 1930's?

Those were all becoming due starting early 1940, which meant that by late 1939, the Nazis had to invade somewhere and hope that the spoils would be enough at least for a partial payment of the money owed. Otherwise, the entire economy would have crashed.

Question: Why was Germany unable to the use resources and manpower in the lands it captured in WW2?
Answer: A conqueror can’t very well use the manpower of captured areas, especially when you have spent a decade spreading propaganda about how inferior and fit for genocide that manpower is. The manpower is not only reluctant, but they will actively sabotage anything they’re set to do. And about the most stupid thing you can do is, of course, to arm them. (It’s telling that Russia has armed Ukrainians that have been press-ganged into fighting in the Russian occupation army. What could possibly go wrong in this scenario? The Russian Army is, as is well-known, the only people on the planet more stupid than Donald Trump.) As for the resources, it’s simply that the Nazis sucked big time at logistics. Yep, despite their own propaganda, which many people believe to this day. They way they did things was to just issue completely unrealistic orders; the people tasked with achieving whatever it was knew that if they failed, repercussions would be severe; hence, they reported success, regardless of the actual outcome. Pretty much like the Soviet Union, actually. The end result was that they scavenged occupied territory for everything, and then sent it on to the front, without taking compatibility into account: they had dozens of makes of vehicles, all with their own spare parts, all the way down to nuts and bolts. That’s a logistics nightmare, and what you get is chaos, and lorries that are standing still here because the bolts for attaching the wheels are the wrong size for the rims, and you can’t get the proper bolts shipped because the lorries there are also standing still because they need the wheels that were delivered here. This organisational ineptitude is built right into Nazism at the most fundamental level; the way Nazis did anything was to create two organisations to do it and let them fight over resources, so that their backstabbing each other would prevent them from ganging up and overthrowing the people in command of both organisations. It was their founding management theory; doing it any other way was considered impractical, wasteful, and outright immoral.

Question: What are the most accurate movies about Nazi Germany, Hitler, and/or WW2?
Answer: “Downfall”, hands down. It’s mainly based on the memoirs of Traudl Junge, Hitler’s private secretary, as written down just after the end of the war, when the events were fresh in her memory. Other eyewitness accounts are also used. There’s one drawback: it only covers the last 10 days of Hitler’s life. Those 10 days were extraordinary, even for being Nazi Germany. Honourable mention to Das Boot, about a German WWII submarine crew. It doesn’t actually take place in Germany, though, and there’s not much about Nazism in it – it’s about the horrors of war in a submarine. And that was, indeed, what WWII was like for a submarine crew: they raced around under the surface and got shot at a lot. Politics and concentration camps didn’t feature in their war.

Name: Mats Andersson
Question: Since Europa has a massive ocean under the ice surface, is it more likely there are giant sea creatures on Europa beneath the surface or no? And why? What kind of giant sea creatures could be on Europa?
Answer: It is incredibly unlikely that there are “giant sea creatures”. As in, there is plenty of reason to believe there aren’t. What you need to have for a thriving ecosystem is energy. Lots of easily accessible energy. Life uses differences in energy levels, and siphons a small percentage off whenever a system goes from huge differences in energy levels to small differences in energy levels. That small percentage goes towards building biological structures. On Earth, that’s sunlight. High energy sunlight comes in, low energy IR goes out, life uses sunlight to build carbohydrates, and the energy that’s stored that way drives the entire cycle of life here. On Europa, what you have under a substantial ice layer is not light. It’s the energy from volcanic vents. Low energy to start with, small energy differentials to live off. There’s simply not enough energy available to sustain a large amount of biomass: the size of life is unrelated to the size of the ocean, it’s got to do with available energy. If there is life, it is overwhelmingly likely to be only microbes. That’s what Earth was like for billions of years, you know. Larger creatures need oxygen (or some other very reactive element) to run a metabolism; there is no photosynthesis to drive oxygen production without sunlight. It would be a sensation of the first rank of there was a microscopic worm to be found anywhere in the ocean. It’s not impossible, because it doesn’t actually violate any laws of physics, but even if there are microbes, the odds are very much against anything bigger.

Name: Mats Andersson
Question: Why wasn’t the small populated and defencless Scandinavia conquered by the Holy Roman Empire and later the German empire?
Answer: Because until WWII, it was a logistical impossibility to support a foreign army in Scandinavia. This is what Scandinavia mostly looks like. There’s a reason why the population is small. There’s nothing to eat. The land you’re seeing here has an inch or two of topsoil, except the areas with no trees, which are bogs. In most places, rocks poke out of the soil, from small ones you can hold in your hand to large boulders that you’ll need several teams of oxen to shift. Patches of the ground look green, because moss is green and can grow directly on rocks without any soil. Up until WWII, armies were heavily into supporting themselves off the land. You need serious forest skills to support yourself off this land, and if you bring an entire army, it’s simply not doable. If you have to ship all supplies from Germany, they’ll spoil before they are halfway. You can’t get an army and its supplies here until you’ve invented the internal combustion engine. And once the army is here – good luck finding an enemy to fight.

Question: Why did Britain not declare war on the Soviet Union in 1939?
Answer: Thanks for the A2A. The Soviets’ official explanation for sending troops to Poland was to defend Poland against the German aggression. It wasn’t a totally unreasonable explanation, and facts on the ground were extremely hard to come by. Remember, this was a time and place when the way to pass on information was normally by mail or courier (even radio was usually extremely restricted; private radio transmitters needed special permits that were normally simply not granted, even into the 1970s in Western Europe; telephone and telegrams would be very unreliable and not always available even in peacetime except for at post offices), and any British envoys in eastern Poland would face enormous difficulties even gathering halfway reliable information about the situation.

Name: Mats Andersson
Question: How did ancient European societies such as the Pre-Viking, Balto-Slavic, and Finno-Ugric settle disputes if they did not have a legal system or customary law like the Greco-Romans, Germans, and Celts? Did they use force to see who was right?
Answer: Thanks for the A2A. Why on Earth do you imagine they had no laws? They weren’t written down, because they had no writing, but they had people who were tasked with remembering them; it was a highly respected position. The earliest laws we have are obviously just someone getting the idea of writing all of it down – the laws must have been developed for centuries or millennia before that. Before laws were formalised, it’s a safe bet that they didn’t use force; we haven’t found a human society yet where this is the norm. What you would most likely do was to ask the shaman to seek guidance from the spirits, or simply gather the tribe and make a common decision on a case-by-case basis. But now we’re talking several thousand years in the past, and we’re firmly into speculation. Fun Fact: where I live, we still have in force a small handful of laws that go all the way back to the first ones that were written down after the Viking era. My own favourite regulates the relationship between older and newer villages, although I can’t actually understand how, due to the archaic language.

Question: Who was the most competent leader or official in the Nazi regime?
Answer: Albert Speer, hands down. Of course, he was a competent architect. Anything else he did, he was just an ordinary person, as competent as the next man. This made him stand out next to the other leading Nazis, who were invariably people who were abject failures until they found an organisation where incompetence mattered less than hating the right people and kissing some major ass. I mean, look at the contenders. Hitler – failed art student, undistinguished in any academic field, got promoted to corporal in the army for basically managing to stay alive while everyone around him perished. Failed as political commissar during the short-lived Bavarian Soviet Republic. Göring – drug addict; spent time in mental institutions due to his addiction and other psychological issues. Goebbels – wanted to be a soldier but was rejected due to his handicaps (club foot, walked with a brace and a heavy limp all his life), failed to get published as an author, which was his lifelong dream. Himmler – having failed as a chicken farmer, he went on to be the butt of jokes for the entire Nazi party, when he wasn’t volunteered for the most gruesome tasks like running the Holocaust. I could go on, but you get the picture. Those were people who had grandiose dreams, all the way up to suffered from delusions of grandeur, and had been cruelly put down by reality. Speer had genuine talent, and was press-ganged into doing something for which he wasn’t qualified, but which he at least approached in a serious manner.

Question: Did Hitler really kill himself or just disappear like Henoch and Allies make up the story, because they couldn't have explained what had happened with him, the same with Himmler?
Answer: All eyewitness accounts say pretty much the same thing: Adolf and Eva Hitler retreated to a private room in the bunker in Berlin on April 30th, 1945; shortly thereafter a gunshot was heard; upon entering the room, Hitler’s staff found them both lifeless – him with a gunshot wound to the head, her smelling strongly of cyanide. Both corpses were carried outside, doused with large amounts of petrol, and burned. Soviet troops later recovered fragments of a skull, with teeth that matched Hitler’s dental records. It also matches several eyewitness accounts of Hitler repeatedly stating that he intended to stay in Berlin rather than flee, and that he did not wish to get captured and suffer the indignity of standing trial for his crimes. Any accounts to the contrary were originally spread by Stalin, who seems to have wanted Western intelligence agencies to look for a possibly surviving Hitler, instead of being busy investigating what the Soviets were up to. Of course, the prospect of Hitler having survived and possibly rallying support for a comeback was sort of scary at that point. I’m not certain why you bring up Himmler; he was in Allied custody when he committed suicide by cyanide. This is well documented and no one has even tried to concoct a conspiracy theory around it.

Question: Could Hitler have won a free election in postwar Germany (50s, 60s) if he was still alive, healthy, and free to candidate?

Hitler got 44% of the votes. He cheated as much as it is realistically possible to cheat, and got less than half of the votes. And that was before he lost a major war. That sort of thing tends to put a dent in your popularity. I say no: he couldn’t even win an election when he was dictator and before things started going seriously downhill for him.

Question: Did Hitler lead the war alone?
Answer: Yes and no. He was supportive of input from his generals, even advice that contradicted him, as long as it concerned purely military matters. In that sense, it was a group effort. The decision was always his. The Nazi way of doing things had a total and absolute ban on delegation; it was seen as inefficient and often even immoral. The Nazi war effort was more akin to a major corporation being led by an obsessively micromanaging CEO, promoted way beyond his abilities but still listening to advice. It wasn’t until the end that he became totally delusional, probably helped on the way by drugs, extreme stress, and possibly some unspecified illness (there is quite solid speculation that he had Parkinson’s, which can lead to cognitive issues and poor mood control).

Question: Why did Hitler invade Europe first instead of invading the Soviets?

Name: Mats Andersson
Question: Could Hitler have avoided Germany's catastrophic defeat at Stalingrad by taking the Caucasus oil instead?
Answer: Well, yes and no. “Avoided catastrophic defeat” no, “at Stalingrad” very possibly. Historians have been all over this with magnifying glasses. The Nazis would, in this scenario, have been completely unable to turn the crude oil into fuel and transport it to where they needed it. In addition, Soviet industrial capacity would have been in better shape, with no need to dismantle entire factories and rebuild them in Siberia. It seems like lots of people want to find one single event that the war turned on. There is no such event. There are a number of events where the Nazis were incredibly lucky, and if you only look at maps, you might form the opinion that one more lucky break, one bad decision less, and they might have won. In reality, it took a lot of effort and a lot of lives, but it wasn’t even close. The Nazis were never going to win, no matter what. They didn’t have the manpower, they didn’t have the industry, and they absolutely didn’t have the logistics. They were too corrupt, too autocratic, and their management theories were insanely incompetent.

Question: Why hasn't the world run out of oil yet? Crackpot Jimmy Carter warned us that the world only had 30 years of oil left-----50 years ago.
Answer: Oil reserves have always been enough to last us for 30 years. Odd, huh? No, not really. You see, there’s a quiet part: it’s not “oil reserves”, it’s “known oil reserves”. And guess what: oil companies send out people to look for more oil. Once they’ve discovered enough so that it’ll last for 30 years, they stop looking, because what happens later is going to become relevant when the current set of employees have all retired, so it’s clearly Someone Else’s Problem. Once the known reserves are down to 27 years or so, they send out new people. There’s more that goes into this, of course. Better extraction methods (for some value of “better”). More efficient engines. The whole supply-and-demand thingymajig that can suddenly make it profitable to extract oil that’s difficult to get to. Renewables, which are better for a whole raft of reasons, lowering demand. But ultimately, it’s because there’s no point in looking for oil once you’ve found enough to last you 30 years.

Question: What does 'det var så lagom roligt' mean?

You could have phrased this famous T-shirt “Kafka hade så lagom roligt”, instead of “Kafka hade inte heller så roligt” (“Kafka didn’t have a lot of fun, either”).

Name: Mats Andersson
Question: What is the national fruit of Sweden?
Answer: There’s nothing official, as such, but I’m offering you this: The wild strawberry. Everyone in Sweden has done this: you find a good, sturdy straw, pick the berries and thread them onto the straw, and then you eat them off the straw. The Swedish word is smultronstrå. And we have the word smultronställe, a place where wild strawberries grow; the meaning is “hidden gem”. The plants are tiny and easily missed; they are not common, but not at all rare either – it’s just that it’s rare that you get more berries in one place than you see in the picture. The taste reminds you slightly of strawberries, but it’s much more intense, sweeter, and, well, a strawberry tastes like plastic next to those. Having them in the garden – the wild variety, not the much blander and sourer cultivars – was what convinced me that my house was the one where I wanted my kids to grow up.

Question: Can we shoot the nuclear waste into Interstellar space to safely get rid of it from the Earth?

Name: Mats Andersson
Question: Why do criminal Swedish gangs commit so many crimes in Denmark?
Answer: I’m reminded of the Danish Windshield Phenomenon. A few years ago, Danish drivers started to complain that as they were driving from Copenhagen to the Swedish port in Ystad, to take the ferry over to the Danish island of Bornholm, people were standing on bridges across the motorway, dropping stones that broke their windshields. Danish police and media were furious with Swedish police and Swedish authorities for not cracking down on the crimes. They accused Swedish police of racism, among the gentler accusations. Question: Why didn’t the rich Nordic countries develop their own nuclear weapons?
Answer: Denmark and Norway don’t have nuclear power plants, which means they have no access to the fissile material needed to build one. Finland was always careful not to worry the Soviets. Developing nuclear weapons would have been a major worry, and would likely not have ended well – or rather, by the Soviets issuing a note to the effect of “Stop doing that, or we will stop you doing that.” We Swedes actually had an active nuclear weapons programme, but abandoned it with the ratification of the Non-proliferation Treaty in 1970. It was later revealed that research on our small cache of weapons-grade plutonium went on for a few years, presumably while the plutonium still was weapons-grade – it’s radioactive enough that it decays into non-fissile material over a time span of years up to a couple of decades. We are today considered a “turn of the wrench” state: we have pretty much all the knowledge needed, and all that’s required is to gather the necessary material and assemble it. Estimates say “less than two years”, which probably means “six months in a pinch”. Unless they already assembled a few and just haven’t tested them yet. Of course, if it had been me doing the planning, I would have constructed a handful of “Little Boy”-type charges, using U-235 and a gun-type mechanism. U-235 has the advantage over plutonium that it’s got a half-life of some 700 million years, so you don’t ever need to replace the fissile material; the gun-type bombs are simple and sturdy and don’t need much in the way of maintenance. Then, in the general confusion of 1991–1992, I’d smuggle them into various places around St. Petersburg, Kaliningrad, and Moscow, equipped with remote detonation. No advanced delivery system needed; the devices are already where they need to be. Then again, I’m a right bastard. Politicians are, of course, made of gentler stuff and would never do such a thing.

Question: Do Russia’s thousands of nukes guarantee that Russia will for many more centuries remain a relevant and powerful nation despite its shrinking population and economy?
Answer: No, absolutely not. A nuke doesn’t just sit there like a monument. The electronics need maintenance; it degrades just by being there. The plutonium (or whatever you use) has such short half-life that it turns into an inert piece of metal after about 30 years and must be replaced – it can’t explode anymore. And don’t get me started on the missiles. The fuel is unstable, with a shelf life of some 6 months. You can’t keep it in the missile, since it’s corrosive and will eat through fuel lines and tanks. And the missile has its own electronics, slowly decaying. Keeping nukes is expensive. You need all that stuff, highly specialised and advanced, plus experts to maintain it all. It is widely assumed that many Russian nukes are no longer working, because they don’t have the resources, and because the officers steal the money for maintenance. Worst case for Russia, the nukes work but the missiles don’t, so they go off sitting in their silos… With the economy going badly and a brain drain like the world has never seen, Russia has maybe 20 or 30 years as a nuclear power. Best case. Worst case, they are no longer a nuclear power already today.

Question: Around what year and month in WW2 was it clear that the USSR had everything under control and was going to sooner or later win the war?

To outside observers, and most Soviets, it was clear after the Battle of Stalingrad, which ended in February 1943. After that, the Nazis had lost too many soldiers and too much equipment, and the tide had visibly turned. With the benefit of hindsight, and access to accurate numbers that neither of the countries had at the time, it was clear in June, 1941. The Nazis could never win; they didn’t have the manpower or the industrial base. They had vastly underestimated the Soviet manpower, industry, and reserves. The Nazis’ main asset was that they had managed to convince everyone that they were much stronger than they actually were; their one chance was to convince the enemy that resistance was futile. Question: If I am a Viking in the Middle Ages I will force captured Christian women as my soldiers' concubines to expand my forces and conquer Christian land, why the Viking only focus on raids, is it an ethical thing or other consideration?
Answer: You’re thinking about this the wrong way. You’re thinking country. You’re thinking that if you go ahead with that plan, your employed soldiers will have huge families that carry on the family tradition 30 years from now. You might not be around, but your heir will. Now… First of all, the Vikings didn’t have countries the way we have. They had a chieftain, and other chieftains had sworn allegiance to him. To him personally. Not to his descendants. The allegiance was dissolved on death. The chieftain could not tax anyone. Had he raised the idea, he’d be a head shorter before the next morning. So he couldn’t employ a warrior class; he had a handful of thugs to protect him, that was all. The hand-to-mouth agricultural economy simply couldn’t sustain an administration or an army. The only way to do anything resembling conquest was to gather the crew for a few ships, in exchange for part of the loot. The Viking expeditions were, in essence, a primitive form of limited company: you put in what you could afford, which for a major chieftain could be a few men, some pelts, and a sail, or something, and for a poor farm, a strong young man with an axe, and you got a part of the profit proportional to what you put in. The plan hardly ever stretched beyond returning from the expedition, because that would be the limit of the agreed cooperation… and also because they were high risk ventures, not something you built long term plans around. So basically, it’s “other consideration” on steroids: you don’t have a society or an economy where your plan is even an idea they can have, much less something they can actually pull off. Also, you wouldn’t normally capture grown women. Children from 5 or 6 up to 10–12 were ideal: small enough to be easily subdued, big enough to perform useful tasks. Any concubining happened later.

Question: Why do Russians call Czars "Tsars" sometimes? How is it spelled in Russian letters?
Answer: “Czar” and “tsar” are simply two different transcriptions of the Russian word “царь”. When you want to represent a word written in a different alphabet, you use certain rules. Those rules differ by language: they are designed to make a speaker of the target language pronounce the word as close to the original as possible. That’s why the last Soviet leader’s name is written “Gorbachev” in English and “Gorbatjov” in Swedish. If you pronounce them by English and Swedish rules, respectively, you end up with similar sounds that are decent approximations of what the name sounds like in Russian. For czar/tsar, it’s a bit more complex, since the title has been in use for quite some time in many languages and morphed a bit along the way – it’s a bit more like how “Moscow” is actually a pretty poor rendering of “Москва”. But ultimately, it’s still just an effort by speakers of various languages to repeat what Russian-speakers say. Incidentally, “царь” is what happens when Russians try to pronounce “Caesar”. The Germans got it more right: “Kaiser” is much closer to how the Romans pronounced the name than the common English pronunciation.

Question: Are capitalism and socialism/communism mutually exclusive or mutually inclusive? How and why?
Answer: The way those words are used in Marxist theory, yes, they are incompatible. “Capitalism” describes any system where you can earn money just by having money. In more practical terms: a system where you can have the stock market or, say, ownership of a factory as your only source of income. Note that owning and managing a factory isn’t in itself “capitalism”: the manager goes to work every morning and does a job, drawing a salary. The key is that it’s possible to sit on your hands and let the money do the working for you. “Socialism” and “communism” are systems where this is impossible, by design. The systems are designed to make this impossible, in various ways. In more common usage, though, people say “capitalism” when they actually refer to a market economy. That means that goods and services are sold on an open and free market. A market economy is not necessarily incompatible with all implementations of Socialism or Communism, although the desired end state will supersede the market economy, and money will cease to exist since it’s no longer expected to be needed as a “rationing system”. For more info about that last part, look up “post-scarcity ecocomy”. If we ever become technologically advanced enough to get anything by pressing a button, we’re going to need some serious re-design of our societies and our ways of thinking: something akin to Communism will be implemented of its own accord, not by political decisions. There is a definite etymological connection to Gotland and the modern provinces of Östergötland and Västergötland. They were never expelled. Their descendants still live here. Sone of them might have moved south at some point to take part in the era of migration around 500 CE, but we don’t know where they started out from. If some of them left present-day Sweden in search of greener pastures, this was some 700 years before Sweden existed. By 500 CE, there was probably not yet a Svea tribe, which Sweden would subsequently be named for; there were certainly no Swedes, since that’s when the last component that would later amalgamate into Swedes arrived. They were not integrated fully until 250–300 years later, when the Viking Age started; we can talk of Swedes only after Birger Jarl’s great project succeeded in the later half of the 13th century. So, in short: no, because they weren’t expelled and no Sweden existed that they could be expelled from.

Question: I got accepted to work in a Swedish HVB home as a personnel. How long will I be able to work there?
Answer: Thanks for the A2A. Says on your contract. It’s either a temporary job, a fixed term job, or a permanent position. The Swedish formal term for a permanent position is, oddly, “tills vidare” – “until further notice” – which is an expression you would otherwise use about something temporary. The informal term that anyone would use in normal speech is “fast anställning”, “fixed employment”. If there’s an end date specified in the contract, well, that’s the end date. Very often, your contract will initially be a probationary contract (“provanställning”). They evaluate you for 6 or 12 months (legislation tends to go back and forth), and if they don’t say anything else, it gets converted to a permanent position at the end of that period. During the probationary period, they can basically terminate the contract for whatever reason just by saying “it’s not working out”; you get two weeks’ notice. For a permanent job, you have a legal right to stay on until you are 69. After that, it’s up to the employer; you can keep working as long as you both agree. I’d say it’s unlikely that an HVB home would actually want you to stay on; the job is somewhat physical.

Question: Why is the gap between the physical strength of men and women so large? If the goal of any species is to survive, wouldn’t it make more sense for women to evolve to be closer to men in regards to physical strength as to better protect their children?
Answer: Sexual dimorphism in mammals is closely related to mating strategies. Species where one male monopolizes mating with several females have big size differences. Our close relatives gorillas have gone down this road: males hold harems of females, and males are easily twice as big as females. This is because the big danger to the males’ reproductive success is other gorilla males, not predators or even starvation. Species where mating is more 1:1 have less size difference between males and females. Our closest relatives, chimpanzees, are like this: they are not exactly monogamous, more like equal opportunities promiscuous, but the point is that males don’t keep harems, and they are basically the same size as females. As for humans, it seems that our earliest ancestors, like australopithecus, had harems: males were a lot bigger than females. It was a competitive edge against other males. This is important in order to understand biology and evolution: competition is always fierce within a species, not so much against other species. Since then, males have shrunk, probably reflecting how our childrearing strategy with extremely long childhoods has made it necessary to have both parents cooperate to raise kids. Since the evolutionary pressure for equal size is rather weak, males are still some 10–20% bigger although we seem to have been predominantly monogamous for a long time. As for “better protect their children”, that’s a team effort for humans. The entire village protects them. Humans are uniquely cooperative; together with pointed sticks, this has made almost all predators on the planet fear humans. And the same cooperative spirit has made it very unlikely for a male to kill a new partner’s children: humans care for all children – even for kittens. Just google it and you’ll see.

Question: Regarding the theory of gradual evolution, how can populations of partially evolved individuals survive their "death sentence" of being handicapped? Isn't evolution the "survival of the fittest"? The partially evolved animal is easy prey, right?
Answer: Wrong. You see, the whole “partially evolved” idea is wrong. At every point, you have an animal which is a slight improvement on what came before. A well-known example is the eye. You start out with a light-sensitive patch on the skin. This way, the animal can know whether it is in the open (potentially dangerous; something might eat it) or hidden beneath something (safer; it’s harder to find). Two patches is better: you can start to “see” which direction light is coming from, and in which direction it is darker. If the patches are in dimples on the skin, the direction sensing gets much better. If they are in a deep recess, it gets even better and you can even get something like an image of the surroundings, with light and shade. A transparent membrane protects your proto-eyes… and this goes on, until you have fully functioning eyes. Every stage is an improvement. There is no such thing as “partially evolved” – all the proto-eyes are useful, and good enough for the animals’ purposes. And we know this because every time the eye gets improved, there’s a part of the population that stays behind, and they are still around – hiding under rocks, in the case of the light-sensitive patch. It’s good enough if all you want to do is to hide from the light. Those two things – gradual improvement and “good enough” – is what is missing from your description. Every step along the way has to improve on what was already there. But your description actually shows why there are still apes – another thing that mystify people with only the sketchiest knowledge about evolution. If apes tried to evolve into humans – or rather, something “human-like” – now, when we are already around, they’d be out-competed in no time at all. They’d be rather bad at being apes, and rather bad at being humans, and they wouldn’t have a “place” of their own in the ecology to occupy. They’d have to do something different – maybe become carnivorous, or living in water, or something else that humans didn’t do. “Omnivorous, savannah-dwelling tool-wielder” is already taken.

Question: Of the sci-fi concepts such as faster than light travel, teleportation, and false gravity on space craft (without it spinning), or other, which is the least likely/furthest away?
Answer: That depends on the exact flavour of each of those things. As far as we know, FTL travel throught a “wormhole” is not forbidden by the laws of physics. There might still be an unknown law forbidding it, and it seems a wormhole can’t be stable for long enough to send an object through it, but FTL communication would still be on the cards, as per current knowledge. (Also, we wouldn’t have the faintest clue how to create one, much less manipulate it.) And then we have hypotheticals like the Alcubierre drive, which requires a form of matter we have good reasons to believe doesn’t exist, but no solid evidence against. Teleportation in the shape of the Star Trek “transporter” isn’t as insane as it sounds. What they do is to take you apart atom by atom, scan the exact quantum state of each atom, and then – depending on SF franchise – either send the atoms one by one to be re-assembled at the destination, or just send the information and assemble locally available atoms into an exact copy, indistinguishable even on the atomic level. Absolutely insanely complex, to the point of probably never being possible in practice, but not actually forbidden by the fundamental laws of physics. Whether the copy is actually the same person, though, is a matter for philosophers. (I would tend to say “no”, although I can’t quite articulate why… except by saying you’re never stuffing me inside one of those things.) Artificial gravity is so far off the table that you hardly ever even read about it in SF novels. It only exists in TV and movies, and even so, only as a handwave explanation for why the actors aren’t floating around the room. There is absolutely nothing that would lead us to suspect gravity can be manipulated that way.

Question: If during the handshake one of them has a cut on his hand, is there a risk of getting HIV?
Answer: Thanks for the A2A. First of all, of course, the person with the cut has to be infected with HIV. Since most people aren’t, that’s your first line of protection right there. And even in case the person with the cut is infected, it is really only a significant risk for medical staff, who will regularly come in contact with other people’s bodily fluids several times every day. What has to happen is for the infected person’s blood to get inside the uninfected person’s body, in some way other than through the mouth. (Our digestion is very hostile to viruses and bacteria; only the hardiest will manage to survive, and HIV viruses are very fragile. I absolutely don’t recommend ingesting HIV infected blood, but I am not aware that HIV has ever been proven to have been transmitted that way.) So, if you shake hands with someone who bleeds all over you, there is a small risk. This is not likely to happen, because most people with cuts will bandage their wounds before they start shaking hands with people. Blood does not get through the skin, so a small amount on your hand is not really dangerous if you wash it off as soon as it’s practical. If the cut is not actively bleeding, of course, there is no risk. Realistically, you are only at danger if you are also bleeding. And even so, the whole point of bleeding is that the blood flows out of the body, preventing viruses and bacteria from entering, so the risk is still low. You’re only at significant risk if you shove the bleeding hand up your anus (or vagina, if you have one). That way, the infected blood will stay in contact with your mucous membranes for a prolonged period, and virus particles might get through, especially since there is a risk that the membranes will tear if you put a hand where it does not really fit. This is not what I would mean by a “handshake”, though. So, realistically, the answer is “No”, since at a minimum, you will have to actually get blood on you for any infection to take place. Otherwise, there is not even a theoretical risk. I don’t think you’ll shake hands with someone who is bleeding. If there is a bandage, plaster or the like on the wound, that is all the protection you need. If the wound is not bleeding, but has a scab of some sort, that is all the protection you need.

What happens is that the cells in the developing embryo are totally insensitive to the hormones that are supposed to turn the embryo into a male foetus. In the absence of those, the embryo “defaults” to female. All mammals function like this. The child that is born will look 100% female. The individual will go on to have a vagina, have wide hips, develop breasts, have no beard, the whole lot that tells you “biologically female” – except for one small difference on the inside: no ovaries. Instead, there are undeveloped testicles that don’t produce testosterone. Most people with androgen insensitivity go through their entire lives not knowing they have a Y chromosome. They are, for all intents and purposes, women – only they are sterile, since they don’t have ovaries. If they go to have an examination regarding their childlessness, it might reveal the truth; in the case of the Algerian boxer, it was determined via a gene test (and subsequent examination, of course).

My ancestors survived the Black Death, so I am probably more resistant to Yersinia pestis infection than e.g. the average Native American, and by sheer coincidence, that tweak to the immune system also gives increased resistance against HIV infection. We still evolve. It’s just that we’re only some 250 generations from the dawn of history – which has given us as much opportunity to evolve as your average E. Coli bacteria strain has had since Tuesday morning.

Question: Why do independent countries still prefer once their master’s language?
Answer: Practicality. Colonies are administrated in the language of the colonial masters. This means that after liberation, they still have a huge number of civil servants who know how to administrate… in the language of the colonial power. At the same time, the colony might have any number of indigenous languages. Nigeria has hundreds. How to choose one to run the country? It is often easier to just keep the colonial power’s language. That way, there is a minimum of change that needs to be done, and no one needs to feel at a disadvantage. In many former colonies, there is also a secondary common language: the trade language. In much of Africa, for instance, the administrative language is English or French, but the trade language is Arabic or kiSwahili.
